To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) experimentally induced change in the valence (i.e., positivity) of attributes contained in stereotypes influences implicit prejudice toward a group, and (2) experimentally induced increase in the positivity of a group (i.e., prejudice) influences implicit stereotypes of that group.

(a) the valence of the attributes contained in a stereotype shapes prejudice toward the group associated with the stereotype, and (b) prejudice toward a group shapes the valence of stereotypic attributes.
(a) the valence of group-stereotypes influences implicit prejudice toward that stereotype and (b) implicit prejudice influences the valence of the group-stereotype.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the processes underlying the relation between stereotypes and prejudice and shows that the valence (i.e., positive or negative) of a group (i.e., a stereotype) influences the valence of evaluations (i.e., prejudice) toward the group and that the valence and direction of evaluations (i. e., prejudice) toward a group (i. e. a stereotype) influences its valence (i. e, the stereotype)
the processes underlying the relation between prejudice and stereotyping, and provides evidence that the relation is bidirectional and based on the congruity of group, valence, and attribute
the relation between implicit stereotypes and implicit prejudice and demonstrates the bidirectional causal nature of this relation
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
prejudice and stereotypes are two different concepts, which are related to each other in a bidirectional causal manner.
stereotypes influence prejudice, but also that prejudice influences stereotypes.
the valence (positive or negative) of attributes associated with a particular group is an important predictor of the extent of prejudice toward that group, and vice versa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
prejudice and stereotypes are conceptually distinct but functionally interdependent constructs.

the valence (i.e., positive vs. negative) of the attributes contained in a stereotype (i.e., the attributes that are associated with a group) influences evaluations of the group (i.e., prejudice), while prejudice toward a target group influences the valence of the attributes contained within the stereotype of that group.

the valence (positive or negative) of the attributes associated with a target influences the evaluation (positive or negative attitude) of the target and the valence of the target influences the attributes associated with the target (i.e. stereotype).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the balance-congruency principle can be used to predict the direction of causal relations between prejudice and stereotypes.
the balance-congruence principle provides a framework for understanding the relation between prejudice and stereotyping. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
